Per-call pricing always looks great on the landing page and terrible in the post-mortem. We used a service like this for address validation. At $0.002 a call it seemed like a rounding error, right up until a retry loop in one of our workers went sideways over a weekend and we woke up to a four-figure bill. Their support was nice about it and gave us a partial credit, but the real lesson was that we had handed someone else's meter a direct line into our infrastructure's failure modes. Every bug became a billing event.

The deeper problem is that it pushes customers into defensive engineering that has nothing to do with the product. We ended up building a caching layer, a dedupe queue, and a hard daily cap with alerting, just to make the costs predictable enough for finance to sign off. At that point you've written a decent chunk of the thing you were paying to avoid writing. I'd happily have paid more in total for a flat tier with a generous ceiling and a soft overage, because predictability is worth real money to anyone who has to forecast a budget.

To be fair, I get why founders do it. It aligns revenue with usage, it makes the free tier easy, and it looks great on a chart for investors. But if you're building one of these, please ship spend caps, per-key rate limits, and usage alerts on day one, not as an enterprise add-on. The customers who stick around are the ones who never had a 3am surprise.

Congrats on the launch. The write path looks genuinely interesting, and I appreciate that the README leads with the tradeoffs instead of a wall of benchmark charts. That said, the first thing I look for with any new database is the durability story, and I couldn't find a clear answer in the docs. When you say a write is "committed," does that mean fsync'd to the local disk, replicated to a quorum, or just acknowledged in memory with a background flush? Those are three very different products, and plenty of databases have earned a bad reputation because the default behavior was quietly the third one.

I'd also love to know whether you've run it through Jepsen, or anything similar, under network partitions and clock skew. "Inspired by Raft" covers a lot of ground. The hard bugs usually aren't in the happy-path consensus logic. They live in membership changes, snapshot installation, and the interaction between leader leases and GC pauses. Even a short write-up on how you test for linearizability would go a long way toward earning trust from people who have been burned before.

Not trying to be a downer. The embedded mode alone could be a big deal for edge deployments where SQLite almost works but you need replication. I just think the projects that make it in this space are the ones that are boringly explicit about failure modes early on, so here's hoping you get there.

I've had a Google Home in my kitchen since 2017, and it's genuinely worse now than it was then. Back in the day I could say "set a timer for 12 minutes" and it just did it. Now about one time in five I get "Sorry, I didn't understand that," or it starts playing a song with "twelve" in the title, or it asks which device I mean when there is literally one device in the room. Basic smart home control has gotten flakier too. "Turn off the lights" sometimes gets "Okay, turning off 14 devices" and sometimes gets nothing. Same phrasing, same room, same lights.

My theory is that these products moved from deterministic intent matching to LLM-backed pipelines. That's great for open-ended questions nobody actually asks their kitchen speaker, and terrible for the three commands everyone uses forty times a day. There also seems to be no organizational incentive to keep the boring stuff working. Nobody gets promoted for "timers still work," and the teams that built the reliable version have presumably been reorged twice since. Meanwhile every response now comes with a little upsell tacked on: "By the way, did you know you can..."

What frustrates me most is that the hardware is fine and the old behavior was fine. If they'd frozen the 2018 firmware I'd be a happy customer. Instead I'm slowly being trained to just use my phone, which I suspect means that in a few years they'll look at engagement metrics, conclude nobody wants voice assistants, and kill the product line.

The old system was dumb but it was predictable, and predictable is exactly what you want from a device in your kitchen. Now it tries to be smart and is worse in the things that actually matters.

I went back to using physical switches and a cheap kitchen timer. Feels little bit like going backwards, but honestly my life is less annoying since then.

It depends almost entirely on what you mean by "slow." If you measure time from first commit to merge, then yes, review adds latency, sometimes a lot. But that was never the number that mattered. What I've seen on every team I've worked with is that the real cost isn't the review itself; it's the queueing. A 20-minute review that sits untouched for two days is a process problem, not a review problem. Teams that treat "unblock your teammate" as higher priority than "start my next ticket" rarely complain that review slows them down.

The other half is PR size. People who hate code review are usually submitting 1,500-line diffs and then getting either a rubber stamp or a week of back-and-forth. Neither is useful. Small, focused changes get reviewed fast and actually get *read*, which is where the value comes from: catching the bad migration, spreading context so you're not the only person who understands the billing code, and keeping the codebase from drifting into five different styles.

I'll grant that for very small, very senior teams, mandatory blocking review can be overkill. Ship-then-review or pairing can work fine there. But "review slows us down" is usually a symptom of big PRs, unclear ownership, or reviewers who nitpick formatting a linter should handle. Fix those and review is mostly a rounding error on cycle time.

The part that always gets me is how the consent dialog is framed. "Allow location access to see weather in your area" is technically true. It's just not the whole truth, which is that your coordinates get pinged every few minutes and shipped to an SDK from a broker you've never heard of. Then that broker resells it to three more. Nobody reading that prompt thinks they're agreeing to have their commute, their gym schedule, and the address they sleep at most nights packaged into a "anonymized" dataset.

And the anonymization claim is the real joke. There's a reason the de Montjoye paper from 2013 keeps getting cited: four spatio-temporal points are enough to uniquely identify 95% of people. If a device spends 11pm to 7am at one house and 9 to 5 at one office building, you don't need a name field. Journalists have repeatedly bought these datasets off the shelf and pinpointed specific individuals, including people at sensitive locations like clinics and military bases.

I don't think the fix is better consent screens, because no amount of UX will make people meaningfully understand downstream resale chains. The fix is making the sale itself illegal or at least liable. As long as the data is worth more sold than kept, every free app with a location permission is a candidate for this.

Every few months we get another one of these and the comments are always the same: "but it's anonymized." It isn't. Location data can't be meaningfully anonymized. Where your phone sleeps at night and where it sits 9-5 on weekdays is basically your name and address. There have been multiple papers showing a handful of points is enough to re-identify most people. This has been known for over a decade.

What actually annoys me is the consent theater. Nobody installing a weather app or a prayer times app thinks they're agreeing to have their movements sold to a data broker who'll resell to whoever pays, including people tracking clinic visits. "We disclosed it in section 14.3 of the privacy policy" is not consent in any sense a normal person would recognize. And the app store review processes clearly don't care.

Anyway, revoke background location for basically everything, check which SDKs are bundled in the apps you use (Exodus Privacy is good for Android), and stop assuming a free app with a location permission is just being helpful. Not a real fix, but until there's actual regulation with teeth, that's what we've got.

+1 from me on dropping Python 3.7. It reached end-of-life in June 2023, so it no longer gets security patches. Keeping it in our CI matrix costs build time and blocks us from cleaning up the codebase. Several of our dependencies have already dropped 3.7, so we're pinning older versions just to keep it working, which carries its own risks. Moving the minimum to 3.8 (or even 3.9, given that 3.8 is also EOL now) would let us use `importlib.metadata` without the backport, simplify our typing imports, and remove a handful of compatibility shims.

For the rollout, I'd suggest we announce it in the release notes for the next minor version and set `python_requires` accordingly. Pip will then keep resolving the last compatible release for anyone still on 3.7. Our download stats show 3.7 usage is a small fraction of installs at this point, so I don't expect much disruption. Happy to help with the PR to update the CI config and packaging metadata if that's useful.

**Tips for Selling Handmade Candles Online? Here's What Worked for Me**

Hey everyone! I've been selling soy candles online for about two years now and wanted to share a few lessons for anyone just starting out.

First, photography matters more than you think. Natural light, simple backgrounds, and a shot of the candle actually burning made a huge difference in my sales. Customers want to imagine it in their home.

Second, be upfront about safety and burn times. Including care instructions builds trust and cuts down on complaints.

Third, start small with scents. I launched with fifteen fragrances and wasted a lot of supplies. Now I keep six core scents and rotate seasonal ones.

Finally, packaging is part of the product. Sturdy boxes prevent breakage, and a handwritten thank-you note gets people coming back.

What platforms are you all using? I'm on Etsy but considering my own website. Would love to hear your experiences!

**Title: Started learning to code at 35, here's my six-month update**

Six months ago I was a warehouse logistics coordinator who'd never written a line of code. I kept telling myself I was too old, that everyone else started at twelve and I'd never catch up. I finally decided to stop listening to that voice.

I started with free Python tutorials after my kids went to bed, maybe an hour a night. The first month was humbling. I spent three evenings stuck on a missing colon. But slowly things clicked. Last week I built a small script that automates our weekly inventory report, saving my team about four hours.

What I've learned: age isn't the obstacle. Consistency is. My experience actually helps, because I understand real problems worth solving.

If you're on the fence, just start. Write something tiny today. You're not behind. You're exactly on time.

Anyone else here start later in life?

**Re: "Is 35 too old to learn programming?" (again)**

Okay, I see this question pop up like every three days so I'm just gonna answer it once and link it from now on.

No. It's not too old. I started at 35. I'm 37 now and I work as a backend dev. Was it easy? Absolutely not. I did it with a full-time job and two kids, coding at 10pm when my brain was basically soup.

What actually matters: consistency. Not some magical "young brain." An hour a day beats a ten-hour weekend binge you never repeat. Build actual projects, not tutorial #47. Get stuck, google it, get unstuck. That's literally the job.

What doesn't matter: your age, your math grades from high school, whether some 22-year-old on Reddit thinks you're "behind."

Stop asking permission and go write some code. Seriously. I gotta run.

The most common culprits are layer caching and build context size.

**1. Bad layer ordering.** Docker caches each instruction, but a change invalidates every layer after it. If you `COPY . .` before installing dependencies, any source edit triggers a full reinstall. Copy dependency manifests first:

```dockerfile
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
```

**2. Huge build context.** Docker sends your whole directory to the daemon before building. Add a `.dockerignore` excluding `node_modules`, `.git`, build artifacts, logs, and large data files. Check the "transferring context" line in the output; if it's hundreds of MB, this is your problem.

**3. Not using BuildKit features.** Enable BuildKit (default in recent Docker) and use cache mounts so package managers reuse downloads:

```dockerfile
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm npm ci
```

**4. Heavy base images.** Switch to `-slim` or `alpine` variants, and use multi-stage builds so compilers and tooling don't end up in the final image.

**5. CI with no cache.** Fresh CI runners start cold. Use `--cache-from` or your CI's registry/GitHub Actions cache backend.

Run `docker build --progress=plain` to see which step is actually slow before optimizing.

First, measure before fixing. Open React DevTools → Profiler, enable "Highlight updates when components render," and find out *which* components re-render and *why*. Many re-renders are cheap and harmless.

Common culprits and fixes:

1. **State lives too high.** If typing in an input re-renders the whole page, move that state down into the component that needs it.

2. **New object/function references every render.** `style={{...}}` or `onClick={() => ...}` passed to children creates new props each time. Use `useMemo` and `useCallback` *when* the child is memoized or the value is a dependency.

3. **Children not memoized.** Wrap expensive, pure components in `React.memo` so they skip rendering when props are shallow-equal.

4. **Context too broad.** Every consumer re-renders when the context value changes. Split contexts (e.g., separate state and dispatch) or memoize the value object.

5. **Derived state in `useEffect`.** Setting state inside an effect triggers an extra render. Compute derived values during render instead.

6. **Passing children as props.** Lifting static JSX into `children` lets it skip re-rendering when the parent's state changes.

If you're on React 19 with the React Compiler, much of the manual memoization is handled automatically.

- **State living too high up.** If a text input's state sits in your top-level App component, every keystroke re-renders the whole tree. Move state down to where it's actually used.
- **New objects/functions every render.** Passing `style={{...}}` or `onClick={() => ...}` to a memoized child breaks the memo because the reference changes each time. `useCallback` and `useMemo` fix that, but only bother when the child is wrapped in `React.memo`.
- **Context doing too much.** One giant context with user, theme, cart, etc. means anything consuming it re-renders when any piece changes. Split it up.
- **Effects that set state on every run.** Check your dependency arrays.

Also, re-renders aren't automatically bad. React is fast. If nothing feels sluggish, I wouldn't lose sleep over it. And if you're on React 19 with the compiler enabled, a lot of the manual memo stuff gets handled for you.

Yes, for most small web apps SQLite is more than fine. It's often the better choice.

**Why it works well:**
- Zero setup: no server process, no credentials, no network hop. The database is a single file.
- It's fast. Reads are extremely quick, and with WAL mode enabled (`PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL;`) you get concurrent readers alongside a writer.
- It handles far more traffic than people assume. Thousands of requests per second on modest hardware is realistic for read-heavy workloads.
- Backups are trivial (`sqlite3 .backup`, or tools like Litestream for continuous replication to S3).

**Where it gets limiting:**
- Only one writer at a time. Write-heavy apps with lots of concurrent inserts may hit lock contention.
- It's awkward if you need multiple app servers writing to the same database, since it's designed for local disk, not network filesystems.
- There are fewer built-in features for user roles and permissions than in Postgres.

**Practical tips:**
- Enable WAL mode and set a `busy_timeout`.
- Keep write transactions short.
- Use an ORM or query layer that makes migrating to Postgres easy later, if you ever need to.

Backups can be as simple as copying a file, though you should use the built in backup command or a tool like Litestream so you never copy it mid write.

Performance is rarely the problem. SQLite handles thousands of reads per second on modest hardware, and with WAL mode turned on, readers no longer block the writer. The real limit is that only one write can happen at a time. For a typical small site with mostly reads and occasional writes, you will never notice. If you expect many users writing constantly at the same moment, that is when Postgres starts to make more sense.

The other thing to watch is deployment. SQLite wants to live on a local disk attached to one machine. If you plan to run several app servers behind a load balancer, or your host uses ephemeral storage, you will need to plan around that. Set a busy timeout, enable WAL, and keep your queries in one place so switching later stays painless.

Put the major version in the URL path: `https://api.example.com/v1/orders`. It's explicit, easy to route, cacheable, and obvious in logs and docs. Header-based versioning (`Accept: application/vnd.example.v2+json`) is more "RESTful" in theory, but it's harder for consumers to discover and debug.

**Key rules:**

1. **Only bump the major version for breaking changes.** Examples are removing fields, renaming things, changing types, or altering semantics. Adding optional fields or new endpoints is non-breaking, so ship those within the current version.
2. **Design for additive evolution.** Tell clients to ignore unknown fields. Avoid enums that clients treat as exhaustive.
3. **Version rarely.** Every major version is something you must run, secure, and document in parallel. Aim for years between bumps, not months.
4. **Have a deprecation policy before you need it.** Announce timelines (e.g., 12 months). Send `Deprecation` and `Sunset` headers, and email registered developers. Watch traffic per version before shutting anything off.
5. **Consider date-based pinning for frequent change.** Stripe's model works well here. Accounts pin to a dated version, and you transform responses between versions internally. It's powerful but requires real engineering investment.

Start with `/v1/`, change carefully, and treat breaking changes as expensive.

Send Deprecation and Sunset headers on old responses so clients can detect them automatically, and track which API keys still hit the old version so you can contact those users directly.

Avoid versioning individual endpoints separately. It sounds flexible but quickly becomes confusing. Treat the version as a contract for the whole surface, document changes in a public changelog, and resist releasing new major versions often.

**Should Phones Be Banned in Schools?**

Few objects have changed adolescence as quickly as the smartphone. In barely fifteen years, it has moved from novelty to necessity, and it now sits in nearly every student's pocket during the school day. This has prompted a growing debate: should schools ban phones entirely? Phones offer real benefits, but the evidence suggests that schools should restrict their use during instructional time, with sensible exceptions.

The strongest argument for restriction is attention. Learning requires sustained focus, and phones are engineered to interrupt it. A single notification can pull a student out of a lesson, and research on multitasking shows that switching between tasks reduces comprehension and memory. Even a silent phone on a desk can be distracting, because part of the mind stays alert to it. Teachers, meanwhile, lose valuable time policing screens instead of teaching.

Phones also affect the social life of a school. Cyberbullying often spreads during the school day, and hallways and lunchrooms can become quiet rows of students scrolling rather than talking. Several countries, including France and the Netherlands, have introduced restrictions and reported calmer classrooms and more face-to-face interaction.

Critics raise fair objections. Parents want to reach their children in emergencies, and some students rely on phones for medical monitoring, translation, or accessibility tools. Phones can also be useful learning devices for research or quizzes. Finally, some argue that banning phones avoids the real task of teaching responsible digital habits.

These concerns, however, point toward a careful policy rather than no policy. Schools can require phones to be stored in lockers or pouches during class while allowing access at lunch or in emergencies. Students with medical or accessibility needs can receive exemptions, and school-owned laptops or tablets can provide educational benefits without the constant temptation of social media. Digital citizenship can be taught directly, rather than learned through daily distraction.

Ultimately, schools exist to help students think deeply and connect with one another. A thoughtful restriction on phones protects both goals. Students will have the rest of their lives to be online; for a few hours each day, school should be a place where their attention belongs to learning.

**Will Robots Take More Jobs Than They Create?**

Few questions provoke as much anxiety as whether machines will leave humans with nothing to do. Headlines warn of warehouses run by robotic arms, trucks that drive themselves, and software that writes reports faster than any analyst. Yet history suggests that automation does not simply destroy work. It reshapes it. Robots will eliminate many existing jobs, but over the long run they are likely to create at least as many, provided societies manage the transition wisely.

The pessimistic case deserves serious attention. Automation targets routine tasks, and millions of workers in manufacturing, retail, transportation, and clerical work perform exactly those tasks. Unlike earlier technologies, modern artificial intelligence can also handle cognitive work such as translation, customer service, and basic coding. If machines improve faster than workers can retrain, displacement could outpace job creation, at least for a generation. Displaced workers rarely move smoothly into new roles. A fifty-year-old factory worker cannot easily become a robotics engineer.

Still, the historical record is encouraging. In 1900, roughly forty percent of Americans worked in agriculture. Today fewer than two percent do, yet unemployment has not risen to thirty-eight percent. Mechanization freed labor for industries no one in 1900 could have imagined, from aviation to software development. Automation lowers costs, which raises demand and spending power, and that spending creates jobs elsewhere. Robots also require designers, technicians, data specialists, and maintenance crews. Entirely new fields, such as drone piloting and AI ethics, have already emerged.

The real danger is not a permanent shortage of work but an uneven distribution of its benefits. New jobs often appear in different places and demand different skills than the ones lost. Without investment in education, retraining programs, and social safety nets, many people could be left behind even as the overall economy grows.

Ultimately, robots will probably create more jobs than they take, just as previous waves of technology did. The outcome is not automatic, however. Whether automation becomes a story of shared prosperity or deepening inequality depends less on the machines themselves than on the choices people make about how to adapt.

**Will Robots Take More Jobs Than They Create?**

Honestly, I go back and forth on this one. When I first started thinking about it, my gut said yes, robots are definitely going to take more jobs than they make. You see self-checkout machines at every grocery store now, and my cousin who works in a warehouse says half his shift is just watching machines do stuff he used to do. It's hard not to feel a little nervous about that.

But the more I read, the less sure I got. People have been freaking out about machines stealing jobs for a long time. Back in the 1800s, weavers literally smashed factory looms because they thought they'd never work again. And yeah, some of them did lose their jobs. But eventually way more jobs showed up, just different ones. Nobody back then could have pictured a job like "app developer" or "social media manager."

I think that's kind of the point. New technology usually creates jobs we can't imagine yet. Someone has to build the robots, fix them, program them, and figure out what to do with all the data they collect. My uncle used to work on cars and now he repairs the automated equipment at a factory, and he actually makes more money than before.

Still, I don't think it's fair to just say "it'll all work out." The new jobs don't always go to the same people who lost the old ones. If you're 50 and you've driven a truck your whole life, being told to "learn to code" isn't exactly helpful. The new jobs also tend to need more school or training, and not everyone can afford that.

So where do I land? I think robots will probably create about as many jobs as they take, maybe even more over time. The real problem isn't the number of jobs. It's whether regular people can actually get to the new ones. If schools, companies, and the government help people retrain, things could turn out fine. If they don't, a lot of people are going to get left behind, even if the numbers look good on paper.

**Should Everyone Learn a Second Language?**

In an increasingly connected world, the question of whether everyone should learn a second language deserves serious attention. Learning a second language should be a goal for nearly everyone, because it strengthens the mind, opens economic doors, and deepens our understanding of other people.

First, learning a second language benefits the brain. Research has shown that bilingual individuals often perform better on tasks requiring attention, problem-solving, and switching between activities. Juggling two vocabularies and grammatical systems exercises mental flexibility in ways few other activities can. Some studies even suggest that lifelong bilingualism may delay the onset of age-related cognitive decline. These advantages are not reserved for prodigies; they are available to ordinary learners willing to practice.

Second, a second language offers practical and economic advantages. Businesses operate across borders, and employers value workers who can communicate with clients, partners, and customers in their native tongues. Fields such as healthcare, education, law enforcement, and tourism especially need multilingual professionals. Even when a job does not require another language, the skill can set an applicant apart from competitors and lead to higher pay or broader opportunities.

Finally, and perhaps most importantly, learning a language builds empathy and cultural understanding. Language carries the values, humor, and history of the people who speak it. When we learn another language, we begin to see the world through a different lens. We also experience the humility of struggling to express ourselves, which can make us more patient with immigrants and visitors navigating our own language.

Critics argue that English has become a global language, making other languages unnecessary for English speakers. Others point out that language study takes time that could be spent on subjects like math or science. These concerns are reasonable, but they overlook the fact that most of the world's population does not speak English fluently, and that language learning reinforces skills such as memory and reasoning that support other subjects.

While not everyone will become fluent, everyone can benefit from the effort. Schools and communities should encourage second-language learning as an essential part of education, preparing people to think more sharply, work more effectively, and connect more meaningfully with others.

The first comment appeared on a Tuesday, at 2:47 a.m., in a file Mara Okafor had not touched in three weeks.

She had been chasing a memory leak through the payment reconciliation service, scrolling past functions she'd written half-asleep and promptly forgotten, when she saw it nestled above `validateLedgerEntry()`:

`// You always forget to close the connection here.`

She stared at it. The office was empty except for the hum of the server closet and the blue glow of her three monitors. Her coffee had gone cold an hour ago. She checked the git blame. The line was attributed to her, committed at 2:46 a.m. One minute ago.

Mara laughed, a short, brittle sound. She was tired. She'd typed it herself and forgotten, the way she sometimes found her keys in the refrigerator. She deleted the comment, fixed the unclosed connection, because it *was* unclosed, and ran the tests.

All green.

She pushed the commit and went home.

On Wednesday, there were four more.

`// This variable name is a lie. It doesn't hold a count.`

`// Why do you still use nested ternaries? We talked about this.`

`// Line 212 will fail on leap years.`

And at the bottom of `utils.js`, set apart by a blank line as if it wanted to be noticed:

`// Are you sleeping enough?`

Mara pushed her chair back from the desk. Around her, the morning standup was assembling: Devin with his kombucha, Priya already arguing about sprint points. Nobody looked at her. Nobody had been in the repository overnight; she checked the access logs twice.

She opened a new file, blank and white, and her fingers hovered over the keys for a long moment before she typed:

`// Who are you?`

She saved it. She waited.

The cursor blinked, steady as a heartbeat.

Then, below her line, letter by letter, something began to type.

The lights died halfway through the best man's toast, right after he said "and that's when I knew Daniel had finally met someone who could put up with him," so the laugh that followed happened in total darkness, and it sounded different. Looser. Like a hundred people had been let off the hook.

For a moment nobody moved. The string quartet's last note hung somewhere near the ceiling of the old barn and then dissolved. Someone's phone lit up, then another, and soon the room was full of small blue moons held at chest height, swinging back and forth, catching the edges of things: a champagne flute, a bare shoulder, the white tiers of a cake that had cost more than Margaret's first car.

Margaret was the bride's mother, and she was the first to stand.

"It's fine," she announced, to no one and everyone. "It's the generator. Phil, it's the generator."

Phil, her husband of thirty-one years, did not get up. He was sitting very still at the head table, and in the glow of his niece's phone Margaret could see that he was smiling. Not the tight, dutiful smile he'd worn all afternoon. A real one.

"Phil."

"I heard you, Maggie."

Outside, the rain that had been threatening since noon finally committed. It came down hard on the tin roof, a sound like applause that wouldn't stop, and somewhere near the back a child shrieked with pure delight.

The bride, Clara, had not moved either. She sat beside her new husband with her veil pushed back and her hand resting flat on the tablecloth, and when Daniel reached over in the dark and found it, she didn't flinch. She turned her palm up.

Margaret would think about that later. How it was the first time all day her daughter had looked like she meant it.

So this happened at my cousin's wedding last summer and I still think about it, so I figured I'd write it out like a story. Bear with me, I'm not a writer lol.

It was at this barn venue about forty minutes outside of town, the kind with string lights everywhere and mason jars on every table. My cousin Dana had been planning it for like two years. She had a binder. An actual binder with tabs.

The ceremony went fine. Her husband Marcus cried before she even got down the aisle, which got everybody going, and the officiant (Marcus's college roommate who got ordained online) only messed up one name. So far so good.

Then we get to the reception. Dinner's done, the toasts are done, Dana's maid of honor gave a speech that went a little long but whatever. The DJ is setting up for the first dance. Everyone's kind of gathered around the dance floor holding drinks, and Dana and Marcus walk out to the middle, and the DJ starts the song.

And like eight seconds in, everything just goes dark.

Not flickering. Just gone. The music cuts, the string lights die, the AC unit in the corner makes this sad whirring noise and stops. Somebody's kid screams. It was maybe 9:30 so it was full dark outside too, no moon or anything.

For a second nobody says anything. Then you hear Dana go "...are you KIDDING me" in this voice I will never forget.

People start pulling out their phones for flashlights, so now it's like fifty little white lights bouncing around a barn. My uncle Ray is yelling about the breaker box. The venue lady is running around saying "it's the whole road, it's the whole road," which, cool, thanks.

And then Marcus's grandma, who I swear had not said one word all night, stands up from her chair.
